::: {.chapter-lead}
**The central question:** if the simplest program explaining an observation is a powerful guide to prediction, can we build an agent that uses this principle to act optimally in an unknown world? AIXI is a formal answer under ideal assumptions. Its obstacle is not merely slow computation: the ideal agent is uncomputable.
:::

**Questions and exercises:** use the [dedicated practice page](exercises/universal-artificial-intelligence.qmd) to check the distinctions between Kolmogorov complexity, Solomonoff induction, and AIXI decision-making.

## 1. Kolmogorov complexity: the shortest program

Fix a universal prefix Turing machine $U$. The Kolmogorov complexity of an object $x$ is

$$
K_U(x)=\min_{p:U(p)=x}|p|.
$$

It is the length of the shortest program that produces $x$.

- A regular string such as a long run of identical bits can have a short description.
- An incompressible string may require a description close to its own length.
- Changing the reference universal machine changes $K_U(x)$ by at most an additive constant. For finite objects, that constant can still matter.

### Why K is not computable

We can enumerate programs and simulate them. Whenever a shorter program outputs $x$, we improve the best known upper bound on $K_U(x)$.

But we cannot, in general, know that no shorter program will eventually halt and output $x$. There is no algorithm that always returns the exact minimum.

Thus $K_U$ is **upper semicomputable** (approximable from above), but not computable in general. This is a computability barrier, not just a high runtime.

::: {.callout-note title="What a practical compressor gives you"}
A compressor produces a computable description length under a specific representation and coding protocol. That is a useful upper bound on description length in a compatible setup—not the exact Kolmogorov complexity. Practical compression is model- and protocol-dependent.
:::

Primary treatment: Hutter, [Universal Algorithmic Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701125), Section 3.2.

## 2. From shortest programs to algorithmic probability

Instead of selecting only the shortest program, assign weight to every minimal program that produces an output prefix:

$$
M_U(x)=\sum_{p:U(p)=x*}2^{-|p|}.
$$

This is a universal algorithmic mixture (a semimeasure). Short programs receive more weight, while many different programs can support the same observation.

The shortest-program term gives, under the matching universal-machine conventions,

$$
M_U(x)\geq 2^{-K_U(x)}.
$$

The relationship is important, but the two objects are not interchangeable:

- $K_U(x)$ is a shortest description length.
- $M_U(x)$ aggregates the weights of programs that generate the observation.

The universal mixture is lower semicomputable, but not computable exactly. It is not generally a normalized probability distribution; the semimeasure qualification matters.

## 3. Solomonoff induction: predict an unknown source

Solomonoff induction uses the universal mixture to predict the next observation after a history.

The intuition is an algorithmic form of Occam's razor: hypotheses generated by short programs receive larger prior weight, while the mixture retains contributions from many alternative computable explanations.

Under formal assumptions—especially that the true generating distribution is computable—Solomonoff prediction has strong convergence and loss guarantees.

This is a theoretical universal predictor, not a practical instruction to enumerate all programs. Its universal mixture cannot be computed exactly.

## 4. AIXI: turn prediction into action

Solomonoff induction is passive prediction. AIXI adds actions and rewards.

It combines:

1. A universal mixture over enumerable chronological semimeasures, which formally represent possible environment interactions.
2. Sequential decision theory.
3. A policy that chooses actions to maximize expected future reward.

::: {.callout-note title="A note on the environment class"}
The terminology varies across the primary sources. Hutter (2007) describes the prior as a mixture over enumerable chronological semimeasures; Leike and Hutter (2015) formalize environments as **lower semicomputable chronological conditional semimeasures (LSCCCSs)**. These are precise computability classes, not simply “all computable environments”.
:::

At a high level:

$$
\pi^* = \arg\max_{\pi} V^\pi_\xi(h),
$$

where $h$ is the interaction history, $\xi$ is the universal environment mixture, and $V^\pi_\xi$ is the expected future value of policy $\pi$ under that mixture.

**The conceptual transition:** Solomonoff induction predicts what an environment may do; AIXI uses those predictions to decide what to do.

AIXI is not a lossless compressor, a conventional language model, or a practical neural architecture. Its optimality is relative to a formal environment class, reward definition, horizon/discount assumptions and reference universal machine.

::: {.callout-note title="Neighbouring framework: the free energy principle and active inference"}
AIXI does not exhaust agentive frameworks built on prediction. The **free energy principle** (FEP) describes a self-organising system that limits long-run surprise through a variational bound. **Active inference** turns this into a perception-action loop in which the agent can learn (update its model) or act (change its sensations so they match its predictions and preferred states).

Three distinctions keep the frameworks watertight:

- AIXI maximises an explicit reward under a universal mixture; active inference minimises an expected free energy given a generative model and preferred states. These are distinct idealisations, not variants of each other.
- Surprisal (the negative logarithm of a probability), variational free energy (a bound used in approximate Bayesian inference) and prediction error (a model-dependent residual) are not synonyms.
- Neither AIXI nor the FEP follows from predictive compression alone: presenting the slogan "compression = intelligence" as a formal consequence of these frameworks would overshoot the evidence.

Primary reference: Friston, [The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn2787), *Nature Reviews Neuroscience*, 2010. Pedagogical comparison: [Compression revision sheet](compression-revision.qmd) · [Cross-source synthesis on compression and intelligence](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/docs/source-syntheses/compression-intelligence-cross-source-2026-11.md).
:::

### Why AIXI is uncomputable

The ideal universal mixture is not computable exactly, and the optimal sequential decision calculation built on it is also uncomputable.

Leike and Hutter (2015) show that the standard/iterative exact AIXI policy is **not limit computable**. They identify two obstacles: deciding between actions with exactly tied values, and the iterative definition of the discounted infinite-horizon value function, which conditions on surviving forever.

Their construction separates the remedies. Allowing **ε-optimality** avoids the need to resolve exact ties; using a **recursive** rather than iterative value function addresses the infinite-horizon problem. Together these yield a **limit-computable ε-optimal AIXI policy** for an infinite horizon. The tolerance ε(t) can decrease toward zero at a computable rate. This is not a blanket impossibility theorem for useful approximations; exact optimality, tie-breaking, value-function definition and horizon must be distinguished. This recursive ε-optimal variant is **not AIXI(t,l)**: the former changes the value-function formulation and accepts an ε gap, while the latter bounds candidate-policy length and computation time.

Primary source: [Leike & Hutter (2015), On the Computability of AIXI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.05572).

## 5. AIXI(t,l): make a restricted construction computable

Hutter's AIXI(t,l) changes the question. Rather than compute the ideal agent, it constructs an agent that compares candidate policies/programs under explicit resource limits.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $t$ | Maximum computation time per interaction cycle for each candidate policy |
| $l$ | Maximum length of candidate programs/policies |
| $l_P$ | In the later proof-validated formulation, maximum length of proofs certifying valid value lower bounds |

It is therefore misleading to say simply that “the environment is restricted to time $t$ and space $l$”. In the AIXI(t,l) construction, $t$ and $l$ bound candidate policies/programs. Hutter also studies bounded environment models, but that is a related, distinct restriction.

### Construction, at a high level

1. Enumerate candidate programs/policies within the length bound.
2. Enforce the per-cycle execution-time bound.
3. In the later formalization, retain policies with proofs that their value estimates are valid lower approximations.
4. At each interaction cycle, run the candidates on the observed history.
5. Choose the action associated with the highest certified value estimate.

The selected policy can change from one interaction cycle to the next. The proof condition is important: the algorithm does not simply trust arbitrary value claims made by candidate programs.

### The computational cost

The detailed construction gives the per-cycle bound

$$
\boxed{T_{\mathrm{cycle}}=O(t\,2^l)}
$$

The factor $2^l$ reflects the exponential number of candidate binary programs up to length $l$ (up to constant factors).

In the later proof-validated formulation, the setup cost is separately bounded by

$$
T_{\mathrm{setup}}=O(l_P^2\,2^{l_P}).
$$

These are asymptotic bounds with very large hidden constants.

<figure>
  <div class="callout-note">
    **Why it remains intractable:** even though the construction is computable, doubling the program-length bound can roughly square the candidate space. The resource limit removes the computability barrier by restricting the search, but the resulting search is still exponential.
  </div>
</figure>

### What the optimality theorem does—and does not—say

The guarantee compares AIXI(t,l) with a restricted class of bounded candidate policies, subject to the validity/proof assumptions. It does not establish global optimality among all agents, nor does it recover exact AIXI at practical cost.

The 2024 textbook makes the proof-length parameter and candidate-selection procedure explicit. See Hutter, Quarel & Catt, [An Introduction to Universal Artificial Intelligence](https://hutter1.net/publ/uaibook2.pdf), Section 13.2, Algorithm 13.1 and Theorem 13.2.3.

::: {.callout-warning title="Read the exponent carefully"}
The detailed construction and the 2024 theorem give $O(t\,2^l)$ **per interaction cycle**. Do not flatten superscripts into an ambiguous $O(t2l)$, or silently rewrite it as $O(t^2l)$. The later proof-validation setup cost is a separate bound.
:::

## 6. Keep the four levels separate

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  K["Kolmogorov complexity K(x)\nShortest program length"] --> M["Algorithmic probability M(x)\nUniversal mixture over programs"]
  M --> S["Solomonoff induction\nPredict an unknown computable source"]
  S --> A["AIXI\nPredict + choose actions to maximize reward"]
  A --> B["AIXI(t,l)\nComputable resource-bounded construction"]
  B --> C["O(t · 2^l) per cycle\nExponential in program length"]
```

| Object | Main question | Computational status |
|---|---|---|
| Kolmogorov complexity | What is the shortest program for $x$? | Not computable; upper semicomputable |
| Solomonoff mixture | How much universal program weight supports $x$? | Lower semicomputable; not computable exactly |
| AIXI | Which action maximizes expected future reward under the universal mixture? | Exact standard/iterative policy: not limit computable; recursive ε-optimal policy: limit computable |
| AIXI(t,l) | What can a restricted candidate class achieve under resource bounds? | Computable in principle; exponential cost and proof overhead |

## 7. What this does—and does not—tell us about LLMs

The connection to language models is real but indirect:

- Next-token prediction estimates conditional token probabilities.
- Predictive coding can turn those probabilities into code lengths.
- Solomonoff induction replaces a hand-designed model class with a universal mixture over enumerable generators; convergence guarantees are stated under assumptions such as a computable true data-generating measure.
- AIXI adds actions and reward-maximizing planning.
- AIXI(t,l) studies a computable, resource-bounded universal-agent construction.

A Transformer trained with cross-entropy does **not** implement Solomonoff induction or AIXI just because prediction and compression are mathematically related. Its finite architecture, training distribution, objective and inference procedure define a different system.
